screens.title: Cloud Service Models and Security
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we map how cloud service models change the boundary of security responsibility. You will learn the practical differences between Infrastructure as a Service, Platform as a Service, and Software as a Service, and why that distinction determines what your team must manage versus what the cloud provider manages. We’ll use everyday analogies to anchor the ideas: building a house from scratch, renting an unfurnished apartment, and riding a public bus. For each model I’ll show two to three specific security controls that remain with the customer and two that the provider typically manages. Understanding this split is not academic — it drives patching plans, identity and access architecture, incident response scope, and compliance obligations. You will see concrete examples like an EC2 VM that requires OS patching, an Azure App Service where the provider patches the runtime, and SaaS platforms like Microsoft 365 where your focus is user and data governance. By the end you’ll be able to ask the right questions when evaluating a new cloud service: what am I responsible for, and what can I rely on the provider to secure? That question is the heart of designing a resilient cloud security posture.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Cloud Service Models
Cloud Service Models and Security
Why the division of responsibility matters for patching, identity, and data governance.

This lesson clarifies where your team must act and where the cloud service provider takes responsibility. Focus on controls you can influence: OS hardening, secure coding, identity integration, and DLP. Recognize provider-managed controls so you avoid duplicating effort or missing gaps in your incident plans.

In this lesson
  • Define IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS using practical analogies.
  • Map customer vs provider security responsibilities.
  • Design controls and spot common misconfigurations.
Coming up
  • Deep dive: IaaS hardening and common mistakes.
  • PaaS security focus: apps, data, runtime configs.
  • SaaS responsibilities: users, access, and DLP.
Visual concept
IaaS
Customer manages OS, apps, data.
PaaS
Provider manages runtime and OS.
SaaS
Provider manages full stack; you manage data and access.
Explore Key Topics
IaaS hardening — OS patching, NSGs, endpoint protection
PaaS configuration — secure coding, runtime settings, keys
SaaS governance — user access, MFA, DLP policies

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next slides you will practice distinguishing service models, analyzing the evolving shared responsibility model, designing controls according to the service type, and identifying common hardening tasks. First, you’ll learn to clearly name whether a workload is IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS and explain why that matters for patching and configuration. Second, you’ll analyze how responsibility shifts so you can draw the line between provider-managed and customer-managed controls. Third, you’ll design security controls tailored to each model — for example, vulnerability management and OS hardening on IaaS, secure coding and runtime configurations on PaaS, and user access governance and DLP on SaaS. Finally, you will be able to spot common misconfigurations such as unpatched VMs, exposed platform keys, or lax SaaS sharing settings. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you can measure progress. These objectives are practical and actionable: you should finish this chapter able to map responsibilities in a real multi-cloud architecture and prioritize the security tasks your organization must own.

screens.title: What is IaaS?
screens.narratorSegment: Infrastructure as a Service is the most fundamental cloud service model. In IaaS you rent virtual machines, storage, and networking from a cloud provider, but you provision and manage the operating system, middleware, application code, and data. A helpful analogy is renting a car: the rental company maintains the engine and chassis, but you drive the vehicle, control the fuel, and decide what to carry in the trunk. From a security standpoint that analogy maps directly: the provider secures the physical data center, the hypervisor, and the underlying network fabric, while you secure the guest OS, installed software, and any services running on the VM. A concrete example from the source material is an EC2 instance on AWS: you must patch Linux or Windows, install antivirus, configure host firewalls, and apply secure configurations for any running database. A common misconception is thinking that moving to the cloud removes the need for host-level security; it does not. Because you control the OS, you are fully responsible for vulnerability management and hardening. The core takeaway is simple: IaaS gives you maximum control and flexibility, but that control brings an equivalent share of security responsibility. Ask yourself whether your operational processes — patching, configuration management, logging, and endpoint protection — are ready for every new VM you provision.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What is IaaS?
IaaS — definition and analogy
Think: renting a car. Provider maintains the vehicle frame; you drive it and fill it.
  • Customer manages: guest OS, applications, data, patches, endpoint protection.
  • Provider manages: hypervisor, physical servers, networking, and data center facilities.
  • Common tasks: configure security groups or NSGs, harden OS, manage secrets, deploy EDR.
Example
AWS EC2: customer patches OS, installs antivirus, configures firewall rules.
Common mistake
Assuming provider patches guest OS; unpatched VMs remain vulnerable.
Visual: Responsibility stack
Provider: Physical infrastructure & hypervisor
Customer: Guest OS and middleware
Customer: Applications and data
Customer: Network security groups, logging, patching
Key Takeaway

IaaS provides flexibility and control but requires ownership of OS and application security processes.

screens.title: IaaS Security Tasks and Hardening
screens.narratorSegment: When you operate IaaS, several routine processes are crucial to keep your environment secure. Start with an image pipeline and hardened base images: build trusted VM images, remove unnecessary services, and bake in secure configuration so every provisioned instance starts in a known state. Next, apply automated patch management to ensure operating systems and installed packages are updated on a predictable cadence. Complement patching with endpoint protection such as EDR and host-based firewalls configured through security groups or NSGs to reduce lateral movement. Implement configuration management and immutable infrastructure patterns where possible to avoid drift. Logging and monitoring must be enabled at both the host and network layers; ship logs to a centralized system and alert on suspicious behavior. Finally, enforce least privilege for administrative accounts and rotate credentials or use short-lived instance credentials. A common misconception is that network security groups alone are enough; they are necessary, but without OS hardening and patching the VM remains exposed. For example, provisioning an EC2 without patching the OS leaves public-facing services vulnerable even if the instance is inside a restricted subnet. The practical sequence is build hardened image, automate patching, enforce endpoint protections, centralize logs, and apply least privilege — together these form an operational baseline for IaaS security.

keyIdea.title: IaaS hardening steps
keyIdea.text: Harden images, automate patching, deploy endpoint protection, centralize logs, and apply least privilege.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › IaaS Security Tasks
Operational steps for IaaS
A repeatable process reduces misconfigurations and drift.
  1. Harden images: build trusted VM images with minimized services.
  2. Automate patches: schedule OS and package updates and test before rollout.
  3. Deploy endpoint protection: EDR, host firewall, and integrity checks.
  4. Network controls: NSGs/security groups, subnet segmentation, and flow logs.
  5. Logging & monitoring: forward host logs, audit trails, and alerting.
  6. Identity & secrets: least privilege admin accounts and rotated credentials.
Example scenario
If an EC2 backend is public-facing, apply hardened AMIs, enable automatic OS patching, attach an IAM role for short-lived credentials, and ensure NSGs restrict access to required ports. Configure EDR to monitor process creation and suspicious connections.
Pro tip
Use immutable images and orchestration to replace instances instead of manual in-place changes to reduce drift.
Common mistake
Relying solely on network controls while neglecting host patching or EDR.
Key Takeaway

Run a defined operational pipeline: hardened images, patch automation, endpoint protections, logging, and least privilege to secure IaaS workloads.

screens.title: What is PaaS?
screens.narratorSegment: Platform as a Service provides a managed development and hosting environment where the provider maintains the OS, runtime, and middleware, while you focus on application code, configuration, and data. Imagine renting an apartment where the landlord provides plumbing, electricity, and the building — you're responsible for your furniture and what you do inside. In PaaS the provider handles many platform-level tasks like runtime patching and environment availability, which reduces operational overhead. However, the security responsibility shifts to secure coding practices, protecting database connections and secrets, and correctly configuring platform features like authentication, networking, and backups. For example, using Azure App Service, Microsoft patches the OS and runtime, but you must protect your database connection strings, secure A P I keys, and implement proper authentication and authorization within your application. A common misconception is to assume that because the provider manages the platform you can ignore application security; in fact application-layer attacks, misconfigured bindings, and leaked keys remain customer responsibilities. The practical focus for PaaS practitioners is strong application security hygiene, secrets management, and platform configuration review so the reduced host-level duties translate into a truly secure deployment.

keyIdea.text: PaaS reduces host management but shifts accountability to application code, configuration, and data protection.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What is PaaS?
PaaS — definition & analogy
Think: renting an apartment. Landlord handles building systems; you manage your living space.
  • Provider manages: infrastructure, OS, middleware, and runtime environment.
  • Customer manages: application code, data, configuration, and identity within the app.
  • Key security focus: secure coding, secrets management, and properly configuring platform services.
Example
Azure App Service: provider patches the runtime; you secure database connections and API keys.
Misconception
Believing platform management removes the need to secure application logic and credentials.
Checklist for PaaS security
  • Perform code reviews and address OWASP Top 10 risks.
  • Use managed identities or key vaults for secrets; avoid baked-in keys.
  • Configure platform authentication and authorization features correctly.
  • Enable platform logging and monitor runtime behavior.
Key Takeaway

PaaS reduces host responsibilities but increases the importance of secure application design and correct platform configuration.

screens.title: PaaS Security Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Securing PaaS workloads focuses on protecting the application and the data it processes. Start with secure development practices: threat modeling, input validation, and dependency scanning to find vulnerable libraries. Use managed identity features or secret stores so credentials and connection strings are never hard-coded. Configure platform-level settings for encryption at rest and in transit where the service allows toggle controls. Use role-based access for platform management and avoid granting broad permissions to application identities. Instrument application and platform logs and forward them to a central monitoring system for detection and incident analysis. A common error is to leave A P I keys or connection strings in configuration files or environment variables without using a vault; this increases risk if an environment is breached. For example, on Azure App Service you should bind the app to a Key Vault or managed identity to access resources rather than storing the secret in app settings. Finally, test platform-specific features periodically, because the provider manages the runtime but you control configuration choices. In short: secure code, store secrets in a managed vault, configure auth correctly, centralize logs, and test configurations regularly.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › PaaS Security Practices
Practical process for securing PaaS
Follow a workflow from code to runtime configuration.
Develop & Scan
Threat model, dependency scanning, and input validation.
Secrets
Use managed identities and vaults; avoid embedded keys.
Config
Enable TLS, encryption, and platform auth features.
Monitoring
Forward app and platform logs to your SIEM or monitoring stack.
Common mistake
Assuming the provider sets secure defaults for all configurations; always verify settings.
Concrete example
On Azure App Service, bind your app identity to Key Vault for DB credentials, enable diagnostic logging, and use RBAC for resource management. Do not store connection strings in source control or plain app settings.
Key Takeaway

PaaS security is about the app and its configuration: secure code, secrets, and verification of platform defaults.

screens.title: What is SaaS?
screens.narratorSegment: Software as a Service delivers full applications over the internet with the provider responsible for the application stack, runtime, OS, and infrastructure. Your team's responsibility narrows to data governance, identity and access management, and application configuration that controls sharing and visibility. A useful analogy is public transit: the bus company owns and maintains the vehicle and route; you simply board and use the service. In security terms this means the provider manages patching of the application and its platform, but you must ensure user accounts have correct privileges, multi-factor authentication is enforced, and data sharing settings conform to policy. A clear example from the chapter is Microsoft 365 or Salesforce: the vendor secures the application environment but your organization must manage user accounts, enforce MFA, and configure data sharing and DLP policies. A common mistake is failing to review default security settings or letting overly permissive sharing remain enabled. The practical result is that SaaS reduces your operational burden, but you must maintain governance to prevent data exposure through misconfigured users or sharing policies. What is SaaS? means saas providers manage the full stack; customers must govern data, users, and application configuration to prevent data exposure.. In practical terms, provider-managed applications — customer focuses on data and access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What is SaaS?
SaaS — definition & analogy
Think: riding a public bus. Provider manages the vehicle and route; you are a passenger who controls your seat and behavior.
Provider: application stack, runtime, OS, and infrastructure.
Customer: user accounts, MFA, data access, and app configuration.
Example
Microsoft 365 or Salesforce: provider secures app and platform; you secure users, MFA, and data sharing.
SaaS configuration checklist
  • Enforce strong authentication and MFA for all accounts.
  • Define and enforce least privilege for user roles.
  • Configure data loss prevention and sharing restrictions.
  • Audit and review tenant settings periodically.
Key Takeaway

SaaS minimizes host duties but places importance on governance of users, access, and data-sharing settings.

screens.title: Shared Responsibility Model
screens.narratorSegment: The shared responsibility model is a conceptual map indicating which security layers the cloud provider secures and which layers you must secure. Across service models the split moves: in IaaS the provider secures the infrastructure 'of' the cloud — physical servers, networking, and the hypervisor — while the customer secures 'in' the cloud — OS, applications, and data. In PaaS the provider takes on more responsibility, handling the OS, middleware, and runtime, leaving the customer to secure application code, data, and platform configuration. In SaaS the provider manages the application itself, so your responsibilities center on data, user access, and tenant configuration. A helpful way to use this model is to draw a simple stack for any given service and mark which layers you must operate or monitor. A common pitfall is assuming a provider takes on a responsibility they do not; for example, a PaaS provider may patch the runtime, but they will not correct insecure application code. Practically, use the model to design controls: if you're responsible for patching, ensure you have a tested patch pipeline; if you're responsible for identity, integrate the service with your enterprise identity provider and enable MFA. The model is a tool for both architecture and governance — it drives choice of controls, incident response scope, and compliance evidence collection.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Shared Responsibility
Mapping responsibilities by model
Translate the conceptual model into operational ownership.
IaaS
Provider: infra, hypervisor. Customer: OS, apps, data, network configs.
PaaS
Provider: infra, OS, runtime. Customer: app code, data, platform config.
SaaS
Provider: app stack. Customer: data, user access, tenant settings.
Using the model
  • Map control ownership to teams and tools.
  • Design incident response with clear provider contact points.
  • Document compliance evidence owner per control.
Quick exercise
For any service you adopt, draw a three-layer stack and mark which team owns patching, data protection, and access control. Use that map to assign SLAs and playbook steps.
Key Takeaway

The shared responsibility model is a planning tool; use it to assign ownership, not as legal cover for missing controls.

screens.title: Designing Security Controls by Service Model
screens.narratorSegment: Designing controls requires matching the control to where responsibility lies. For IaaS, your control set must include host-level measures: patch management, endpoint protection, filesystem encryption, host-based logging, and network segmentation via NSGs. For PaaS, focus on application controls: secure coding, dependency management, secrets in vaults, RBAC for platform resources, and telemetry at the application layer. For SaaS, prioritize identity and data governance: enforce MFA, integrate with enterprise identity providers, apply least privilege roles, and configure DLP and sharing restrictions within the application. When you design architecture, avoid copying a single control set across models — e. g., treating a PaaS runtime like a set of VMs and insisting on host EDR may duplicate effort; instead, use platform-native telemetry and A P I-based protections. Conversely, do not omit controls just because the provider manages the stack; SaaS still requires strong access controls and audit configurations. Use the shared responsibility map to choose tooling: a vulnerability scanner and patch automation for IaaS, static analysis and secrets scanning for PaaS, and identity governance and DLP for SaaS. The control design should feed your incident playbooks and compliance evidence collection so ownership is clear during an event.

For PaaS, focus on application controls: secure coding, dependency management, secrets in vaults, RBAC for platform resources, and telemetry at the application layer. For SaaS, prioritize identity and data governance: enforce MFA, integrate with enterprise identity providers, apply least privilege roles, and configure DLP and sharing restrictions within the application. When you design architecture, avoid copying a single control set across models — e. g., treating a PaaS runtime like a set of VMs and insisting on host EDR may duplicate effort; instead, use platform-native telemetry and A P I-based protections. Conversely, do not omit controls just because the provider manages the stack; SaaS still requires strong access controls and audit configurations. Use the shared responsibility map to choose tooling: a vulnerability scanner and patch automation for IaaS, static analysis and secrets scanning for PaaS, and identity governance and DLP for SaaS. The control design should feed your incident playbooks and compliance evidence collection so ownership is clear during an event.

screens.title: Common Misconfigurations & How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Across service models some misconfigurations routinely cause incidents. In IaaS, forgetting to patch VMs or leaving default administrative credentials on instances is common and dangerous. In PaaS, storing secrets in configuration files or failing to restrict platform roles causes exposures even when the runtime is patched. In SaaS, permissive sharing settings or not enforcing MFA lets unauthorized users access sensitive data. Avoid these mistakes with clear operational guardrails: enforce automated patching and image hardening in IaaS, prohibit plain-text secrets and require vault-backed secrets in PaaS, and enforce identity federation and MFA for SaaS. Implement periodic configuration reviews and use automated scanners where available — for example, use cloud configuration assessment tools to find publicly exposed storage or overly open role assignments. A common misconception is trusting default settings as secure; defaults vary by provider and many defaults favor ease of use rather than hardening. The preventive pattern is routine automation, least privilege, secrets management, and configuration audits; when combined these practices close the majority of common gaps mentioned in the chapter. Common Misconfigurations & How to Avoid Them means automate patches, vault secrets, enforce mfa, and run configuration audits to prevent common misconfigurations.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Spot-the-Difference: Who Secures This?
screens.narratorSegment: A practical way to test your understanding is the spot-the-difference exercise. You will be given tasks and must decide whether they fall to the cloud provider or the customer depending on the service model. For example: patching the OS on an EC2 VM is a customer responsibility in IaaS; enabling runtime patching on Azure App Service is typically the provider's duty in PaaS; configuring MFA for Salesforce users is the customer's duty in SaaS. When answering, explain the owning rationale: does the task relate to the physical infrastructure, the runtime platform, or application data and users? A common trap is ambiguous phrasing — if the task mentions application-layer logic, it is usually the customer's responsibility regardless of model. Use this exercise to build mental templates: if the task involves physical or hypervisor maintenance, mark provider; if it involves code, configuration, or user accounts, mark customer. After you assign responsibilities, write a short remediation plan that lists the specific tool or process you would use — for instance, automated patch orchestration for IaaS or Key Vault integration for PaaS secrets. This practice converts conceptual knowledge into operational decisions you can apply immediately.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Consolidate your learning with three simple concepts. First, IaaS provides the most customer control: you manage OS and applications while the provider secures the underlying infrastructure. Second, PaaS shifts responsibility upward: the provider handles OS and runtime, leaving you to secure application code, secrets, and platform configuration. Third, SaaS reduces operational duties to data and user governance: enforce MFA, least privilege, and DLP while the vendor manages the application stack. Use the shared responsibility model as a decision tool: draw the stack, mark ownership, and then design controls and operational playbooks to fill the customer responsibilities. Avoid the common mistakes: unpatched VMs in IaaS, exposed secrets in PaaS, and lax access controls in SaaS. A clear mapping of ownership keeps incident response fast and compliance evidence organized. Ask during every procurement: which responsibilities remain ours and how will the provider support logging, alerts, and evidence sharing? That question will help you build a resilient, auditable cloud security posture.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we map how cloud service models change the boundary of security responsibility. You will learn the practical differences between Infrastructure as a Service, Platform as a Service, and Software as a Service, and why that distinction determines what your team must manage versus what the cloud provider manages. We’ll use everyday analogies to anchor the ideas: building a house from scratch, renting an unfurnished apartment, and riding a public bus. For each model I’ll show two to three specific security controls that remain with the customer and two that the provider typically manages. Understanding this split is not academic — it drives patching plans, identity and access architecture, incident response scope, and compliance obligations. You will see concrete examples like an EC2 VM that requires OS patching, an Azure App Service where the provider patches the runtime, and SaaS platforms like Microsoft 365 where your focus is user and data governance. By the end you’ll be able to ask the right questions when evaluating a new cloud service: what am I responsible for, and what can I rely on the provider to secure? That question is the heart of designing a resilient cloud security posture.

Over the next slides you will practice distinguishing service models, analyzing the evolving shared responsibility model, designing controls according to the service type, and identifying common hardening tasks. First, you’ll learn to clearly name whether a workload is IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS and explain why that matters for patching and configuration. Second, you’ll analyze how responsibility shifts so you can draw the line between provider-managed and customer-managed controls. Third, you’ll design security controls tailored to each model — for example, vulnerability management and OS hardening on IaaS, secure coding and runtime configurations on PaaS, and user access governance and DLP on SaaS. Finally, you will be able to spot common misconfigurations such as unpatched VMs, exposed platform keys, or lax SaaS sharing settings. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you can measure progress. These objectives are practical and actionable: you should finish this chapter able to map responsibilities in a real multi-cloud architecture and prioritize the security tasks your organization must own.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and assessment. You will apply the model distinctions to a realistic multi-cloud scenario: an EC2 backend on AWS, a frontend on Azure App Service, and a Salesforce SaaS system. For each component you will state the service model, list customer responsibilities such as OS patching or securing A P I keys, and list provider responsibilities like physical security and runtime patching. The hands-on deliverable is a short table summarizing responsibilities for each component. In addition, you will complete a spot-the-difference exercise where you decide whether a task belongs to the customer or the provider. These practice steps test both knowledge and judgement, because responsibilities sometimes overlap or require negotiation with the provider. A clean mapping lets your team prioritize controls, avoid duplicated effort, and build accurate incident response playbooks. By the end of practice you should be able to produce a simple security checklist for any new cloud service you onboard.

Infrastructure as a Service is the most fundamental cloud service model. In IaaS you rent virtual machines, storage, and networking from a cloud provider, but you provision and manage the operating system, middleware, application code, and data. A helpful analogy is renting a car: the rental company maintains the engine and chassis, but you drive the vehicle, control the fuel, and decide what to carry in the trunk. From a security standpoint that analogy maps directly: the provider secures the physical data center, the hypervisor, and the underlying network fabric, while you secure the guest OS, installed software, and any services running on the VM. A concrete example from the source material is an EC2 instance on AWS: you must patch Linux or Windows, install antivirus, configure host firewalls, and apply secure configurations for any running database. A common misconception is thinking that moving to the cloud removes the need for host-level security; it does not. Because you control the OS, you are fully responsible for vulnerability management and hardening. The core takeaway is simple: IaaS gives you maximum control and flexibility, but that control brings an equivalent share of security responsibility. Ask yourself whether your operational processes — patching, configuration management, logging, and endpoint protection — are ready for every new VM you provision.

When you operate IaaS, several routine processes are crucial to keep your environment secure. Start with an image pipeline and hardened base images: build trusted VM images, remove unnecessary services, and bake in secure configuration so every provisioned instance starts in a known state. Next, apply automated patch management to ensure operating systems and installed packages are updated on a predictable cadence. Complement patching with endpoint protection such as EDR and host-based firewalls configured through security groups or NSGs to reduce lateral movement. Implement configuration management and immutable infrastructure patterns where possible to avoid drift. Logging and monitoring must be enabled at both the host and network layers; ship logs to a centralized system and alert on suspicious behavior. Finally, enforce least privilege for administrative accounts and rotate credentials or use short-lived instance credentials. A common misconception is that network security groups alone are enough; they are necessary, but without OS hardening and patching the VM remains exposed. For example, provisioning an EC2 without patching the OS leaves public-facing services vulnerable even if the instance is inside a restricted subnet. The practical sequence is build hardened image, automate patching, enforce endpoint protections, centralize logs, and apply least privilege — together these form an operational baseline for IaaS security.

Platform as a Service provides a managed development and hosting environment where the provider maintains the OS, runtime, and middleware, while you focus on application code, configuration, and data. Imagine renting an apartment where the landlord provides plumbing, electricity, and the building — you're responsible for your furniture and what you do inside. In PaaS the provider handles many platform-level tasks like runtime patching and environment availability, which reduces operational overhead. However, the security responsibility shifts to secure coding practices, protecting database connections and secrets, and correctly configuring platform features like authentication, networking, and backups. For example, using Azure App Service, Microsoft patches the OS and runtime, but you must protect your database connection strings, secure A P I keys, and implement proper authentication and authorization within your application. A common misconception is to assume that because the provider manages the platform you can ignore application security; in fact application-layer attacks, misconfigured bindings, and leaked keys remain customer responsibilities. The practical focus for PaaS practitioners is strong application security hygiene, secrets management, and platform configuration review so the reduced host-level duties translate into a truly secure deployment.

Securing PaaS workloads focuses on protecting the application and the data it processes. Start with secure development practices: threat modeling, input validation, and dependency scanning to find vulnerable libraries. Use managed identity features or secret stores so credentials and connection strings are never hard-coded. Configure platform-level settings for encryption at rest and in transit where the service allows toggle controls. Use role-based access for platform management and avoid granting broad permissions to application identities. Instrument application and platform logs and forward them to a central monitoring system for detection and incident analysis. A common error is to leave A P I keys or connection strings in configuration files or environment variables without using a vault; this increases risk if an environment is breached. For example, on Azure App Service you should bind the app to a Key Vault or managed identity to access resources rather than storing the secret in app settings. Finally, test platform-specific features periodically, because the provider manages the runtime but you control configuration choices. In short: secure code, store secrets in a managed vault, configure auth correctly, centralize logs, and test configurations regularly.

Software as a Service delivers full applications over the internet with the provider responsible for the application stack, runtime, OS, and infrastructure. Your team's responsibility narrows to data governance, identity and access management, and application configuration that controls sharing and visibility. A useful analogy is public transit: the bus company owns and maintains the vehicle and route; you simply board and use the service. In security terms this means the provider manages patching of the application and its platform, but you must ensure user accounts have correct privileges, multi-factor authentication is enforced, and data sharing settings conform to policy. A clear example from the chapter is Microsoft 365 or Salesforce: the vendor secures the application environment but your organization must manage user accounts, enforce MFA, and configure data sharing and DLP policies. A common mistake is failing to review default security settings or letting overly permissive sharing remain enabled. The practical result is that SaaS reduces your operational burden, but you must maintain governance to prevent data exposure through misconfigured users or sharing policies. What is SaaS? means saas providers manage the full stack; customers must govern data, users, and application configuration to prevent data exposure.. In practical terms, provider-managed applications — customer focuses on data and access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Third, SaaS reduces operational duties to data and user governance: enforce MFA, least privilege, and DLP while the vendor manages the application stack.
